title: Equity Method vs Consolidation: Accounting for a Stake You Don’t Control
summary: Equity method vs consolidation, decided cleanly: the control test, the significant influence test, how the one-line method works, and when the answer changes.
body_markdown:
## The Three Ways to Report a Stake in Another Company


Equity method vs consolidation is not a percentage question. It’s a control question, and it runs in a fixed order. Accounting for a minority stake in another company means landing on one of three reporting models, and you get there by running two tests in sequence.


Never start at the cap table.


**Step one. Do you control it?** ASC 810-10-15-8 makes ownership of a majority voting interest the usual condition for a controlling financial interest, and more than 50 percent of the outstanding voting shares points toward consolidation. The same paragraph is explicit that control can also exist at a lesser percentage, through contract, lease, agreement with other stockholders, or court decree. ASC 810-10-15-8A carries the model into limited partnerships, where control turns on kick-out rights rather than a share count.


The presumption breaks in one direction that catches operating companies constantly. Under ASC 810-10-25-11, noncontrolling rights that let the minority holder effectively participate in selecting, terminating, and compensating management, or in setting operating and capital decisions, are substantive participating rights. They overcome the majority holder’s presumption to consolidate. A 60 percent owner whose partner can veto the budget and fire the CEO does not consolidate. It uses the equity method.[BDO’s blueprint on control and consolidation under ASC 810](https://www.bdo.com/getmedia/8a458199-b9e0-4445-8b0e-f8f1bd7a180f/Control-and-Consolidation-Under-ASC-810.pdf) works through the voting interest model.


**Step two. Do you have significant influence?** ASC 323-10-15-8 governs, and that test gets its own section below.


**Step three. Neither?** Equity securities short of significant influence are measured at fair value through net income under ASC 321-10-35-1. Where the investee has no readily determinable fair value, ASC 321-10-35-2 permits an election to carry it at cost minus impairment, adjusted for observable price changes in orderly transactions for the identical or a similar investment of the same issuer. That election gets reassessed every period and ends the moment a readily determinable fair value appears.


Consolidation (ASC 810) Equity method (ASC 323) Fair value or alternative (ASC 321)


Trigger Controlling financial interest Significant influence, no control Neither


Presumption More than 50 percent voting 20 percent or more of voting common stock Below 20 percent, influence not demonstrated


Balance sheet Every asset and liability One line, investment in investee One line, fair value or cost less impairment


Income statement Every revenue and expense, then NCI One line, equity in earnings Fair value and observable price changes


Investee revenue in your top line Yes No No


Investee debt on your balance sheet Yes No No


A fourth path ignores ownership entirely. ASC 810-10-15-14 defines a variable interest entity by insufficient equity at risk, equity holders without power over the activities that most affect economic performance, or disproportionate voting and economic rights, and ASC 810-10-25-38A consolidates the holder with both power and significant economics. Sometimes at zero percent ownership. Run that assessment first when the structure looks unusual.


Noncontrolling interest is the mirror image of this fact pattern. NCI arises when you consolidate a subsidiary you only partly own, and it sits inside consolidated equity under ASC 810-10-45-16. Here you’re the minority holder looking in, not the parent looking down. Each path produces a different set of[GAAP financial statements](https://www.indinero.com/resources/gaap-guide/) .


## The Significant Influence Test


The significant influence 20 percent test is a presumption, not a threshold. It’s rebuttable in both directions.


ASC 323-10-15-8 sets both halves. An investment of 20 percent or more of the voting stock presumes the investor can exercise significant influence, absent predominant evidence to the contrary. Below 20 percent, the presumption is that it cannot, unless the ability can be demonstrated.[PwC’s guidance on the significant influence presumption](https://viewpoint.pwc.com/dt/us/en/pwc/accounting_guides/equity_method_of_accounting/Equity_method_account/chapter_2/21_significant_influence_presumption.html) is blunt that these are general guidelines rather than bright lines, and that 20 percent versus 19.9 percent is not a substantive distinction.


### What creates significant influence (ASC 323-10-15-6)


ASC 323-10-15-6 lists the indicators of that ability:


1. Representation on the board of directors
2. Participation in policy-making processes
3. Material intra-entity transactions
4. Interchange of managerial personnel
5. Technological dependency
6. Extent of ownership relative to the concentration of other shareholdings


Item six is the one operators miss. A 12 percent stake sitting alongside 88 percent spread across 200 holders is a completely different animal from a 12 percent stake sitting next to a single 88 percent founder. The CPA Journal has noted that ownership as low as 3 percent can require the equity method where the investor in fact exercises significant influence, and that the SEC applies no bright-line test. Note also that the standard asks for the ability to exercise influence, never for proof that it was exercised. A passive 25 percent holder who has never attended a meeting still qualifies unless something affirmatively took the ability away.


### What overcomes the presumption (ASC 323-10-15-10)


ASC 323-10-15-10 lists five circumstances that can defeat a 20 percent-plus presumption:


1. Opposition by the investee, such as litigation or regulatory complaints, challenging the investor’s ability to exercise significant influence
2. An agreement, such as a standstill agreement, under which the investor surrenders significant shareholder rights
3. Majority ownership concentrated among a small group that operates the investee without regard to the investor’s views
4. The investor needs more financial information than other shareholders receive, tries to get it, and fails
5. The investor tries and fails to obtain board representation


ASC 323-10-15-11 makes clear the list is illustrative, that no single item is conclusive, and that predominant evidence across all facts and circumstances is what it takes. Read items four and five closely. Both require the investor to have actually tried, which makes this a documentation obligation rather than a conclusion you reach in your head. The indinero team writes that memo when the position goes on the books, so it’s in the file before[audit preparation](https://www.indinero.com/blog/audit-preparation/) starts.


### LPs and LLCs run on a different threshold


This is the most common technical error in mid-market books. The 20 percent presumption applies to common stock and in-substance common stock of a corporation, and to LLCs that don’t maintain separate ownership accounts. For limited partnership interests and for LLCs that do maintain specific ownership accounts, the SEC staff position at ASC 323-30-S99-1 requires the equity method unless the interest is so minor that the limited partner has virtually no influence over operating and financial policies. Practice reads that more-than-minor bar as roughly 3 to 5 percent. A 6 percent LP interest in a real estate partnership is an equity method investment. A 6 percent common stock position generally is not.[Deloitte’s roadmap on equity method investments and joint ventures](https://dart.deloitte.com/USDART/home/publications/deloitte/on-the-radar/equity-method-investments-jv) covers the same split, and it’s worth checking every partnership and LLC interest on your balance sheet against it.


## How the Equity Method Works in Practice


The equity method of accounting starts at cost and then moves with the investee. The ASC 323 equity method produces one balance sheet line and one income statement line, and everything below happens inside them.


### Cost first, then the basis difference


ASC 323-10-30-2 requires initial measurement at cost, applying the ASC 805-50-30 cost accumulation guidance. A step-up into the method from ASC 321 is adopted prospectively under ASU 2016-07, so the day-one carrying amount is the previous basis plus the cost of the new interest, with no restatement of prior periods.


Say you paid 2,000,000 for 30 percent of an investee whose book equity is 5,000,000. Your share of underlying equity is 1,500,000. The 500,000 gap is the basis difference, and it is not a plug. ASC 323-10-35-13 requires it to be accounted for as if the investee were a consolidated subsidiary, which means a hypothetical purchase price allocation as of your investment date, tracked in memo accounts that never touch your balance sheet.


Component Amount Amortized?


Fair value step-up on equipment, 8-year life 160,000 Yes, 20,000 per year against equity in earnings


Customer relationship intangible, 5-year life 200,000 Yes, 40,000 per year against equity in earnings


Deferred tax liability on the step-ups (90,000) Unwinds with the related assets


Equity method goodwill (residual) 230,000 No


Equity method goodwill isn’t amortized under ASC 350 and isn’t separately tested. It rides inside the single investment line, captured by the ASC 323-10-35-32 other-than-temporary impairment test on the investment as a whole. Skip the allocation and you overstate the earnings pickup by 60,000 a year until an auditor catches it.


### The running entries


ASC 323-10-35-4 states the objective plainly. Recognize your share of investee earnings or losses in the periods the investee reports them, adjust the carrying amount for that share, and reduce the carrying amount by dividends received.


Event Debit Credit


Initial investment Investment in investee 2,000,000 Cash 2,000,000


Pickup of 30 percent of 900,000 net income, less 60,000 basis amortization Investment in investee 210,000 Equity in earnings 210,000


Dividend received Cash 90,000 Investment in investee 90,000


Share of investee OCI Investment in investee 15,000 Other comprehensive income 15,000


That distribution is basis coming back. Booking it to dividend income double-counts, because the earnings that funded it were already picked up.


Two mechanics belong in the same monthly checklist. Investee period ends rarely match yours, so a reporting lag is normal. ASC 323 sets no limit, and practice applies the ASC 810-10-45-12 three-month tolerance by analogy on two conditions: the lag stays consistent, and material intervening transactions still get recognized or disclosed. Changing an established lag is a change in accounting principle under ASC 250. Intercompany profit is the other. ASC 323-10-35-7 eliminates only your proportionate share, not the 100 percent you’d eliminate under ASC 810. Both belong in the standing task list for[closing your company’s books](https://www.indinero.com/blog/business-bookkeeping-closing-your-companys-books/) , alongside the distribution classification election that[ASU 2016-15](https://storage.fasb.org/ASU%202016-15.pdf) requires you to apply consistently to every investee.


### When losses run the investment to zero


ASC 323-10-35-19 requires the investor to keep recognizing losses up to the carrying amount plus net advances, and it reads advances broadly. Capital contributions, additional common stock, preferred stock, loans, debt securities, and other advances all absorb. ASC 323-10-35-24 sets the order, most subordinated first, so common absorbs before preferred and preferred before loans.


ASC 323-10-35-20 then stops the recognition. Once the investment and net advances reach zero, the investor ordinarily discontinues the equity method, unless it has guaranteed obligations of the investee or is otherwise committed to further support. ASC 323-10-35-21 adds a narrow exception where an imminent return to profitable operations appears assured. Suspended losses go into a memo account, and when the investee returns to profit, subsequent income is applied against those unrecognized losses first, in reverse order of absorption. Equity in earnings resumes only after cumulative income equals the losses never recognized.


## When the Answer Changes


Classification is a continuing assessment, not a founding decision. Equity method vs consolidation gets re-answered every time ownership, governance, or the shareholder base moves.


### Crossing into control


When an equity method investor obtains a controlling financial interest in a business, ASC 805-10-25-10 requires it to remeasure the previously held interest at acquisition-date fair value and recognize the gain or loss in earnings. Amounts previously recognized in OCI under ASC 323-10-35-18 get reclassified into the same calculation. The one-line presentation disappears, and every asset, liability, revenue, and expense of the investee arrives on your face financials, plus an NCI for the piece you don’t own.


Two exceptions matter. An acquired set that isn’t a business is an asset acquisition under the cost accumulation model with no remeasurement gain, and a common control transaction isn’t remeasured at all.


### Crossing in and out of the equity method


Moving up from ASC 321 used to require retroactive restatement.[FASB’s ASU 2016-07](https://storage.fasb.org/ASU%202016-07.pdf) struck that, and ASC 323-10-35-33 as amended makes adoption prospective as of the qualification date. ASU 2020-01 added the step most summaries miss. Immediately before applying the equity method, the previously held interest is remeasured under ASC 321-10-35-1 or ASC 321-10-35-2, so if you’d been using the measurement alternative, the transaction that created significant influence is itself an observable price change.


Moving down works the same way. Under ASC 323-10-35-36 the investor discontinues the equity method prospectively without reversing recognized earnings, derecognizes the proportionate share of the carrying amount including related basis differences, remeasures the retained interest under ASC 321, and reclassifies its share of AOCI. Loss of control from the other direction is a deconsolidation event under ASC 810-10-40-5. Neither direction rewrites history, which is exactly why the memo you wrote at the time is the only defense you have.


### What this does to your covenants and your top line


The classification decides which financial statement the investee’s economics live on, and that reaches well past the accounting department.


- **Revenue.** An equity method investee’s revenue never touches your top line. Own 40 percent of a JV doing 20 million in revenue and you report one line of equity in earnings, not 8 million of revenue. Every figure you quote to a lender or a buyer has to match.
- **Debt and covenants.** The investee’s borrowings stay off your balance sheet. Credit agreements often define EBITDA to exclude equity in earnings of unconsolidated affiliates and count only cash distributions received, so read the definition before assuming the covenant model moves with GAAP.
- **EBITDA quality.** Equity in earnings is non-cash. A company weighted toward equity method pickups has a cash conversion story to tell, and any[financial due diligence](https://www.indinero.com/blog/financial-due-diligence/) team will normalize it out.
- **Board visibility.** A one-line pickup tells your board nothing about the investee’s revenue, margin, or liquidity. Supplemental JV reporting is a management choice, not a GAAP requirement, and it’s what[fractional CFO support](https://www.indinero.com/services/cfo-services/) builds before the first board question lands.


Both transitions are disclosure events, and a step acquisition produces a remeasurement gain that’s often large, non-cash, and highly visible.


## Common Pitfalls


Every one of these is diagnosable from the trial balance, and every one of them surfaces in diligence.


1. **Applying the equity method by ownership percentage alone.** Someone reads “20 to 50 percent equals equity method” and stops. The fix is a dated influence memo per investee walking the ASC 323-10-15-6 indicators and the ASC 323-10-15-10 counter-indicators. A 25 percent holder refused a board seat and denied financial information may well be an ASC 321 investor.
2. **Running investee losses below zero.** ASC 323-10-35-20 stops loss recognition when the investment plus net advances hits zero, absent a guarantee or commitment to further support. Both failure modes are restatement candidates, recording losses past zero without a guarantee, and stopping at zero when a guarantee means they should continue.
3. **Recording dividends as income.** The distribution reduces the carrying amount. Booking it to other income double-counts against earnings already picked up and overstates net income by the full amount received.
4. **Ignoring the basis difference.** Cost almost never equals your share of book equity. Skipping the ASC 323-10-35-13 allocation means no amortization of the step-ups, an overstated pickup every period, and an investment line that won’t agree to the ASC 323-10-50-3 disclosure.
5. **Treating a joint venture as a consolidation because the partners share control.** Joint control is the definitional absence of unilateral control. A 50-50 JV is an equity method investment for both venturers, and proportionate consolidation isn’t an available policy choice for the vast majority of US GAAP reporters.
6. **Never revisiting the classification.** A financing round dilutes you from 24 percent to 17 percent. A partner buys out a co-investor. Your board designee resigns. Any of these can move the answer, and none of them generate a journal entry that would prompt anyone to look.


The through-line is documentation, not arithmetic. Indinero’s books are audit-ready by default. Accrual basis, with the judgment written down when it’s made and defensible to your auditor on day one.

## Frequently asked questions


These come up most often on live equity method positions, from the 20 percent presumption to what happens when losses run the carrying amount to zero. Each answer cites the governing ASC paragraph, so you can take it straight to your auditor.


### Does owning 20 percent automatically mean significant influence?


No, the 20 percent test in ASC 323-10-15-8 is a rebuttable presumption, and it’s rebuttable in both directions. A standstill agreement, a denied board seat, or a controlling group that operates without regard to your views can defeat it under ASC 323-10-15-10. Limited partnership and LLC interests run on a different bar entirely, roughly 3 to 5 percent under ASC 323-30-S99-1, and missing that is the most common technical error indinero sees in mid-market books.


### What happens when losses exceed the carrying value of the investment?


Under the equity method, loss recognition stops once the carrying amount plus net advances reaches zero, per ASC 323-10-35-19 and -20. A guarantee of investee obligations or a commitment to further support keeps losses running past zero, and ASC 323-10-35-24 absorbs them most subordinated first, common before preferred, preferred before loans. Indinero keeps a suspended loss tracker with the seniority ordering documented, since equity in earnings resumes only after cumulative income covers what went unrecognized.


### How are dividends from an investee recorded under the equity method?


Dividends received from an equity method investee reduce the carrying amount of the investment on your balance sheet, rather than being recorded as income. The entry debits cash and credits investment in investee, because the distribution is basis coming back, not a return on the period’s earnings. Recording it as other income overstates net income by the full amount received, and it’s the error a buyer’s quality of earnings team finds first.


### What changes when ownership rises from 30 percent to a controlling stake?


When ownership reaches a controlling stake, the equity method ends and ASC 805 remeasures the previously held interest at acquisition-date fair value. The gain or loss runs through earnings, amounts previously in OCI get reclassified, and every asset, liability, revenue, and expense of the investee arrives on your face financials plus a noncontrolling interest. It’s a disclosure event, and the remeasurement gain is often large, non-cash, and highly visible to lenders and boards.


### Is the equity method required for joint ventures?


Yes, a corporate joint venture is generally an equity method investment for each venturer under ASC 323, since no partner controls it alone. Joint control is the definitional absence of unilateral control, so a 50-50 JV lands on one line for both venturers, not consolidated line by line. Proportionate consolidation isn’t an available policy choice for the vast majority of US GAAP reporters, and treating a JV as a consolidation is a restatement candidate.


### How does an equity method investment show up on the cash flow statement?


An equity method investment’s earnings pickup is a non-cash item removed from operating cash flow, and dividends follow an ASU 2016-15 policy election. That election is either the nature-of-distribution approach or the cumulative-earnings approach, and you apply it consistently to every investee. Purchases and sales of the investment itself are investing activities, so a company weighted toward equity method pickups has a cash conversion story to tell its lenders.


### Do small startup investments held by an operating company use the equity method?


Usually not, because most small startup stakes carry no significant influence, so they fall under ASC 321 rather than the ASC 323 equity method. Where the investee has no readily determinable fair value, the ASC 321-10-35-2 measurement alternative carries the stake at cost less impairment, adjusted for observable price changes. SAFEs and convertible notes you hold sit outside ASC 323 until conversion, and ASC 323-10-15-13 covers in-substance common stock, so the classification gets reassessed at every round.
